posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

Where did the antimatter go? The Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other instantly. So why does anything exist at all? Scientists are still hunting for the missing half of reality.

What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. But thanks to new techniques for DNA sequencing, dating ancient detritus, mathematical models, and aerial and lidar archaeology, we are now able to get a faint idea of what this world might have looked and felt like.

Observing the early universe would be such a fascinating and relaxing experience... or would it be?

We imagine advanced alien civilizations building gigantic spaceships, Dyson spheres and empires spanning entire galaxies. But what if true technological progress goes in exactly the opposite direction? Not outward into space, but deeper and deeper into the smallest layers of reality?

What is the Barrow Scale? How powerful could a civilization become by mastering DNA, and even fundamental particles, and could the universe already be filled with godlike civilizations hiding in plain sight? Watch
Let's visit some of the most dangerous neighbourhoods... in space!

recentPosts.caption:
Pokémon fans, this hotel in Japan has a surprise waiting around almost every corner. ⚡️⁠
⁠
MIMARU’s Pokémon Rooms are packed with more than 100 Pokémon hidden throughout the space, from the walls and furniture to little details you might miss at first.⁠
⁠
Guests also get Pokémon-themed items and activities, making the room just as fun as the rest of the stay.⁠
⁠
By: @mimaruhotels

Would you make it through the Cu Chi Tunnels in Vietnam, or get stuck halfway? 💀⁠
Inside the famous underground tunnel network, where some passages are so narrow that squeezing through is a challenge of its own.⁠
⁠
Built and used during the Vietnam War, the tunnels offer a glimpse into the underground life of Vietnamese soldiers at the time.⁠
🎥: @chuck_taylorrr

"Tsingy" is a Malagasy word often translated as "where one cannot walk barefoot". It was first used for Madagascar's sharp limestone forests, and Tsingy Rouge, in the north of the island, takes its name from them. ⁠
⁠
Here the spires are made of soft red earth, carved by rain and river water over time. They are fragile, and each rainy season reshapes them a little.⁠
⁠
By: @goithacatravel @iamcollinsnkem

Serbian food culture is all about generous portions, traditional recipes, and the joy of sharing a hearty meal! ⁠
Grilled meats are a big part of the country's culinary identity, often served alongside fresh salads, warm bread, spicy peppers, and flavorful homemade sides.⁠
⁠
It’s simple, satisfying food rooted in tradition, where the experience is just as much about gathering around the table as it is about the flavors. 🤤⁠
⁠
Would you try Serbian cuisine?⁠
🎥: @balkan.flavors

Award-winning photographer @isabellandscapes takes some of the most incredible nature photos you’ll ever see. ⁠
⁠
She was the first to document the tree-shaped formation in Iceland in 2023 (shown on the cover). ⁠
⁠
The rest of these shots come from her travels around the world, landscapes that look more like paintings than real places. Nature may be the artist, but it takes a sharp eye to find these masterpieces.⁠

A pangolin taking a shower? Now that’s not something you get to see every day! ⁠
⁠
Watching this little creature enjoy a refreshing rinse is definitely an unexpected wildlife moment. ⁠
⁠
🎥: @olionlypans

Photographer @cetashean captured these incredible whale moments from above during golden hour. 🐋⁠
⁠
The photos show three different moments at sea, from a whale breaching through the surface to a young calf breaching alongside its mother and a female following a dolphin.⁠
⁠
Shooting whales from above takes incredible timing, patience, and plenty of luck, making moments like these especially difficult to capture.

In the wild, tiny lives are quietly breathing. Please do not disturb their natural habitats, and please do not share their exact locations on social media.⁠
⁠
This is not a tourist attraction; it is their home. Let’s all raise our awareness and work together to protect these precious little ones.⁠
⁠
🌏 These flying squirrels live in forests all around the world, including the Japanese dwarf flying squirrel in Japan, across northern Eurasia like the forests of China, and the American flying squir

What if every course came with its own soundtrack? ⁠
@sreyahalder shows us an omakase dining experience where the music changes with each dish, making every course feel a little different.⁠
⁠
Omakase is all about trusting the chef to choose what you eat, and here, the experience goes beyond the food by bringing sound into the mix too. ⁠
Would you try a dining experience like this?

The Kayan are an ethnic group from Myanmar, and many families settled in northern Thailand after fleeing conflict. Kayan women are known for the brass coils they wear around their necks, a tradition passed down from mother to daughter for generations. ⁠
⁠
A girl usually receives her first coil at around five years old, and longer ones replace it as she grows. ⁠
⁠
Today, each woman decides for herself whether to wear them. ⁠For the Kayan, the coils are a sign of beauty and cultural identity.

A phone booth turned into your own mini nightclub? 📞🪩 ⁠
Teledisko in Berlin, where you step inside, choose your favorite song and get your own little dance party!⁠
⁠
With colorful lights, music and space just for you, it feels like having an exclusive club all to yourself,  only much smaller. 😂🎶⁠
Would you step inside for a solo dance party?⁠
🎥: @gowithgustodotdotdot

Photographer Samantha Cavet captured these fascinating deer photos at Tapada Nacional de Mafra, an 800-hectare natural park in Portugal that is home to deer and other wildlife. She had always dreamed of photographing deer here and wanted the images to feel soft, almost painterly.⁠
⁠
Samantha focuses on landscapes, nature, and the connection between emotion and place, and the last three slides take us to Madrid, Spain, for more of her nature work.⁠
⁠
Which photo is your favorite? 😍⁠
⁠
By: @saman

For several weeks each fall and winter, schools of migrating mullet can be seen along Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts. To capture the scale and majesty of the annual mullet run, National Geographic Explorer @macstonephoto dropped into the clear waters south of the Everglades, coming face to face with millions of fish in one of North America's largest marine migrations.

Presented by @Rolex. Bearded vultures have a remarkable diet—they feed mainly on bones, which they crack open on rocks. Yet fewer than 400 remain in southern Africa. Raptor conservationist and National Geographic Explorer Shannon Hoffman is using captive breeding to help restore the population. Her team is now reaching a critical stage as some birds reach breeding age. Learn more about the effort to protect these scavengers at the link in bio.

On Kukeri Day, dancers in elaborate masks, animal skins, and bells move through Bulgarian villages and households. These rituals are meant to drive away evil spirits and welcome health, fertility, and prosperity. As the tradition unfolds in Sredets, photographer @ivodanchevphotographer documented three Kukeri performing inside an abandoned, roofless home.

See more Photos of the Day at the link in bio.

Presented by @Rolex. Pangolins usually roll into a ball when threatened, which can protect them even from hungry lions. But this defense mechanism can't protect them from those who hunt them for their meat and, more recently, their scales. Conservationists, like those at the @tikkihywoodfoundation, are taking on the labor-intensive challenge of caring for orphaned and injured pangolins while also working with authorities to stop black-market trafficking of these vulnerable creatures.
